Configuration

Each orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins (Pauli exclusion). Equal-energy orbitals fill singly with parallel spins before pairing (Hund’s rule). The Aufbau principle guides filling of lower-energy subshells first.

Usual filling sequence

Which subshell fills next?

The usual filling sequence is not a universal energy ranking: orbital energies change, and some elements have configuration exceptions.

A noble-gas core stands for the electrons in that noble gas. Fill the remaining occupied subshells; these are not always only valence electrons. Each orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.

General periodic trends

These are general trends: atomic radius usually decreases across a period and increases down a group. First ionisation energy and electronegativity generally show the opposite pattern. Individual exceptions occur.

Period 3

Schematic sizes, not measured radii. Argon is a neutral atom with 18 electrons, like P³⁻, S²⁻ and Cl⁻. Group labels are spaced as categories.

Cations are smaller than their neutral atoms; anions are larger. Within an isoelectronic series, more protons attract the same number of electrons more strongly.

Each point is the energy needed to remove the next electron from a gaseous atom or ion. The highlighted jump begins removal from an inner shell. Argon’s jump occurs at the ninth removal, beyond this eight-electron display.

3 · Overall molecular polarity

Bond dipole arrows point towards the more electronegative atom, with a crossed tail at the positive end. Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of all bond dipoles. Identical outer atoms in a symmetric arrangement can give a nonpolar molecule despite polar bonds. The diagrams are schematic projections: solid wedges project towards you and dashed bonds recede. Lone pairs determine molecular shape but are omitted here. Arrow lengths illustrate directions rather than measured dipole magnitudes. C–H bonds are weakly polar towards carbon in this model; methane remains nonpolar. The SO₂ drawing is a simplified bonding representation of a delocalised molecule. PCl₅ here refers to the gaseous molecular form.

Select a bonded atom to replace its bond with a lone pair. Lone pairs occupy equatorial positions first in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement. In an octahedral arrangement, the first lone pair may occupy any position; the second goes opposite it. Equivalent positions are all accepted. This practice covers the common shapes: up to two, three and two lone pairs for 4, 5 and 6 domains respectively. The diagram is a schematic projection, not an angle scale.

Carbon valence orbitals · promoted-state model

Hybridisation combines orbitals on one atom, not on different atoms. One s plus one, two or three p orbitals gives two sp, three sp² or four sp³ hybrids. Any equivalent choice of p axes is accepted. Remaining p orbitals stay unhybridised and can participate in π bonding. The boxes use the promoted carbon valence-bond model, with one electron in each orbital; this is not the isolated atom’s ground-state configuration. The starting view shows one carbon atom with one s and three p orbitals. Hybrid orbitals appear only after a correct selection is submitted. The surfaces are schematic. Each colour identifies one orbital; both lobes of a p orbital share that colour. Colours do not indicate orbital phase or electrical charge. Hybridisation is a mathematical bonding model, not a literal mixing animation.

Left carbon
Right carbon

Click one orbital on each carbon. Corresponding hybrid orbitals form a σ bond by end-on overlap; parallel p orbitals form π bonds by sideways overlap. Each sp carbon has two unhybridised p orbitals, each sp² carbon has one, and sp³ carbon has none. Two density regions on opposite sides of the bond axis represent one π bond. Only orbitals involved in the carbon–carbon bond are shown; the other hybrid orbitals used for C–H bonds are omitted. The view is a fixed schematic projection, with colours identifying orbital sets rather than phase. Bond selection order is for exploration, not a time-resolved mechanism.

3 · Formal charge

Formal charge compares a neutral atom’s valence-electron count with the electrons assigned to it in a Lewis structure. Split bonding electrons equally: a single bond contributes one owned electron, a double bond two, and a triple bond three. Each lone pair contributes two owned electrons. Formal charge = expected valence electrons − electrons owned. This is electron bookkeeping, not a measurement of actual charge distribution. Individual formal charges are left unlabelled in the diagram for this exercise.

One resonance contributor is shown. Calculate ownership using the bonds and lone pairs in this drawing. The overall ion charge need not equal the central atom’s formal charge.

Complete the resonance structures

Add the alternatives you need. In each new drawing, select its π bond, then the oxygen bond where you want it to move.

Resonance hybrid

The dashed portions show delocalised π bonding. Fractional charge labels are resonance-averaged formal charges, not measured partial charges. Lone pairs are omitted.

Build all equivalent major contributors with complete octets for these examples, including the given structure. Keep atoms and σ bonds fixed. Moving the π bond transfers its pair into a lone pair on the first oxygen while a lone pair on the next oxygen forms a new π bond. Lone pairs and formal charges update together, keeping the total number of electrons and overall charge constant. A π bond contains two electrons. These drawings represent one delocalised species, not molecules switching back and forth. Minor contributors with incomplete octets or additional charge separation are outside this exercise.

RepulsionQualitative interactionAttraction

London dispersion acts between all particles, including polar and hydrogen-bonding molecules. The moving clouds illustrate correlated temporary dipoles and induced dipoles; their fluctuations are schematic. Larger, more polarisable clouds generally give stronger dispersion at a comparable separation. Permanent dipoles favour some orientations and repel in others. A hydrogen bond is shown when a hydrogen covalently bonded to N, O or F points towards an available lone-pair region on N, O or F in the other molecule. Blue dots mark lone pairs and dashed gold lines mark hydrogen bonds; covalent bonds remain solid. At very short distances, electron-cloud overlap produces strong repulsion. The meter is an illustrative radial-interaction model, not a measured force, energy or universal ranking of force types. The molecules are schematic projections with fixed internal geometry.

1 · Which IMFs are present?

Between molecules of the pure substance. Select all that apply.

First select all forces present, then choose the most prominent one. Hydrogen bonding is a specific strong dipole interaction; this activity includes both dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding for suitable polar molecules. This exercise uses the usual school-level classification for small molecules: London dispersion for nonpolar molecules, dipole–dipole for polar molecules without conventional hydrogen bonding, and hydrogen bonding when suitable donors and acceptors are present. London dispersion occurs in every example; the choice does not mean other interactions disappear. Hydrogen bonding requires a suitable donor, typically H directly bonded to N, O or F, and a lone-pair acceptor. An ether or carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds from water without allowing the pure substance to hydrogen-bond to itself. The sketches show connectivity, not exact 3D shapes; methane and CCl₄ are tetrahedral, and NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal. SO₂ is shown with a simplified bonding representation. This classification is not a quantitative ranking of interaction energies or boiling points; size, polarisability and molecular shape also matter.

* marks the incoming hydrogen from H⁺.

Electron-pair donation

Select a bond

A dative covalent bond (coordinate bond) forms when one atom supplies both electrons in the shared pair. The donation arrow goes from the lone-pair donor to the acceptor. The reaction above supplies formation history: after formation, equivalent bonds cannot be distinguished by electron origin alone. In ammonium and hydronium, the star tracks the newly introduced hydrogen, not a permanently different kind of bond. In the silver complex, either ligand-to-metal bond is accepted. The diagrams show product connectivity; donated lone pairs are now bond pairs. Local charges on the boron adducts are formal charges, not measured partial charges. The overall charge is shown for the silver complex. These drawings are schematic rather than exact 3D geometries.

1 · Which way do the electrons move?

2 · Select the electrons to transfer

Scroll sideways to see all atoms.

Extended ionic lattice

A 2D schematic showing the repeating ion ratio, not the exact crystal geometry. The array continues beyond its edges.

Metal atoms lose outer-shell electrons to form positive ions. Non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negative ions. Select electrons on every donating atom when more than one is shown. The number of electrons lost equals the number gained, and the resulting ion charges balance. All electrons within a subshell are indistinguishable; the dots are a simplified shell model. Newly gained electrons are coloured blue only to track the transfer. The formula shown is the simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound, not a discrete molecule. Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, rather than the transfer itself. The diagram illustrates electron bookkeeping, not a complete reaction pathway.

Positive ion coresDelocalised electrons

A smaller cation with a greater positive charge has higher charge density. The model compares charge divided by relative ionic volume, and shows one, two or three delocalised electrons per atom. Stronger metallic attraction generally favours greater hardness and higher melting points, but real properties also depend on crystal and electronic structure. The circles show the relative sizes of common cations as a school-level metallic-bonding model; they are not measured metal-atom sizes, and the diagrams do not predict exact melting points or conductivity.

The upper two rows move right and then down to join the lower two rows, changing a 4 × 4 arrangement into 2 × 8. All sixteen positive ion cores and sixteen delocalised electrons remain. Attraction between the cores and the shared electron sea persists, illustrating malleability. This is an idealised rearrangement, not a force-calibrated deformation simulation. Real metal deformation usually involves dislocations rather than a rigid block following this path.

Pure metal

Alloy

Original atomsAdded atoms

Different-sized atoms distort the regular layers of the alloy and hinder dislocation motion. The closely packed pure-metal layers slide under the applied pressure; the alloy stays fixed within the pressure range represented here. This does not mean alloys cannot deform: enough stress can move dislocations or cause other deformation. The model illustrates size-mismatch strengthening with fixed substitutional atoms. Real alloy behaviour also depends on composition, phases, defects and processing. The small lift during pure-metal sliding prevents the hard-sphere drawings from overlapping; it is not a literal atomic deformation pathway.

1 · Name the longest carbon chain

Hydrogens bonded to carbon are not shown.

Scroll sideways to see the whole structure.

Molecule name

Choose the longest continuous chain (at most eight carbons). It can turn corners. For equally long choices, prefer more side branches. Each side branch is named by its carbon count: methyl, ethyl or propyl. Number from the end giving the lowest set of branch positions, comparing the first point of difference; use alphabetical order to break a remaining tie. Repeated branches use di-, tri- and so on; these prefixes do not affect alphabetical order. Carbon-bound hydrogens are hidden by default; use Show hydrogen to reveal them. The live name shows your current choices, not an answer, until checked.

Hydrogens bonded to carbon are not shown.

Molecule name

These examples contain one principal functional group, with parent chains of up to eight carbons and occasional methyl branches. Functional-group atoms and their hydrogens are drawn explicitly; other carbon-bound hydrogens are hidden by default and can be revealed with Show hydrogen. Select both carbons of C=C for an alkene or C≡C for an alkyne. Their position is the lower of the two carbon numbers. Select O and H for an alcohol; N and both H atoms for a primary amine; C and O for a ketone; C, O and H for an aldehyde; C, both O atoms and H for a carboxylic acid; or C and both O atoms for an ester. The carbonyl carbon belongs to the parent chain. An ester is named as two parts: the oxygen-side alkyl group followed by the acid-side alkanoate. Number the principal group before considering side branches. This is a connectivity diagram, not a molecular geometry model. Alkenes and alkynes use -ene and -yne and give the multiple bond its lowest position. Stereochemistry (E/Z) is not assessed. The name underneath reflects your choices until checked.

Functional Group NamingIdentify a displayed group and practise its name, prefix, suffix or condensed formula. Check any fields you choose.Draw Functional GroupsComplete a fixed molecular fragment by placing atoms and bonds to create the requested functional group.

R and R′ represent carbon groups. Fill in any fields you want to check.

Use the open-chain suffix. For a prefix, treat the displayed group as attached to the left-hand R.

All atoms within the functional group are displayed, including its hydrogens. R and R′ stand for the rest of the molecule and may differ. Prefixes and suffixes depend on the parent structure: this activity uses common open-chain suffixes, and substituent prefixes with any carbonyl carbon outside the parent. For ketones, oxo- replaces two hydrogens on a parent carbon. Esters use an alkyl name followed by an -oate name; alkoxycarbonyl- describes the group attached through its carbonyl carbon. Ethers use an alkoxy- prefix and have no characteristic suffix here. Alkenes and alkynes use -ene and -yne within the parent name; enter none for their characteristic-group prefix. Alkenyl and alkynyl instead name entire unsaturated substituents. C=C and C≡C are accepted as group formulas; –CH=CH– is also accepted for the displayed alkene. Hyphens, spaces and ordinary or subscript digits are accepted. For a bridging condensed group, show both attachment ends, such as –O–.

Carbon-bound hydrogens are omitted. Include O–H, N–H and aldehyde hydrogens; other carbon-bound hydrogens remain implicit, including on alkenes. Lone pairs are not required.

Choose an atom tool and a dotted position to place an atom. Choose a bond tool, then its two atoms; clicking an existing bond replaces its order. Erase removes an added atom and its bonds, or an added bond. The given fragment is fixed. All dotted positions must be filled. This activity checks atom placement and covalent bonds, not lone pairs or three-dimensional geometry. The available examples cover alcohols, primary amines, ketones, aldehydes, carboxylic acids, esters, primary amides, ethers, alkenes and alkynes.
